headline_marked: Police [[use AI to flag 'suspicious' drivers]], leading to pretextual stops, ACLU reports
headline: Police use AI to flag 'suspicious' drivers, leading to pretextual stops, ACLU reports
summary: A new report claims law enforcement uses AI algorithms and license plate reader data to identify motorists with "suspicious" travel patterns, often leading to stops for minor violations.
details: Police are increasingly using AI-derived pretext to justify pulling drivers over, according to an October 26 report by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). Senior policy analyst Jay Stanley states that AI algorithms and automated license plate reader (ALPR) surveillance data flag motorists whose travel histories appear “suspicious.”

This occurs even without evidence of wrongdoing, with officers potentially looking for minor traffic violations to justify the stop. In some documented cases, officers have concealed the actual reason for the stop, implying it was based on AI alerts.

ALPRs photograph vehicles, recording registration, location, and timestamps. By combining data from multiple cameras, law enforcement can track vehicle travel routes and frequency of visits to specific locations.

An AI system analyzes this vast surveillance data to identify patterns it deems "suspicious," triggering alerts. The ACLU expresses concern that this approach will increase "pretextual stops," sweeping in many innocent people.

The report highlights growing concerns about mass surveillance camera networks regarding privacy, potential abuse, and limited regulation. Several officers have been fired for abusing the Flock surveillance system.

While license plate readers have traditionally tracked known suspects, the current scale of blanket surveillance is unprecedented. A network of over 335,000 Flock ALPR cameras exists across the United States.

Companies like Flock Safety are developing AI-enhanced surveillance systems that identify "unusual" travel behavior and vehicle associations, marketing them as crime-prevention tools. These systems can generate new suspects based on behavioral patterns.

topic: uk politician sues xai over deepfake
headline_marked: [[UK Politician Jess Asato sues xAI]] after deepfake images circulated on X
headline: UK Politician Jess Asato sues xAI after deepfake images circulated on X
summary: British MP Jess Asato is taking Elon Musk's xAI to court, arguing unlawful use of her image to create degrading deepfakes. The case could set a precedent for AI company accountability.
details: British Labour MP Jess Asato has initiated legal action against Elon Musk's xAI. She alleges the company unlawfully used her image to create and circulate "disturbing and degrading" deepfake images, with one reportedly depicting a sexual assault.

The lawsuit stems from the "Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025," where xAI's chatbot was reportedly used to generate sexualized images of women and children. Asato reported the deepfakes to X, but the platform allegedly dismissed her complaints.

Asato has a long-standing background campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Prior to entering Parliament, she worked with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children, shaping her political focus on online protections.

The case seeks to establish a legal precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm. Asato is challenging whether consent remains meaningful when AI tools can generate almost any image, and if companies building these tools can be held responsible.
